source.title: CodeBrain: Bridging Decoupled Tokenizer and Multi-Scale Architecture for EEG Foundation Model
source.authors: Jingying Ma; Feng Wu; Qika Lin; Yucheng Xing; Chenyu Liu; Ziyu Jia; Mengling Feng

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling analyses to an EEG foundation model and reports results as EEG training-data volume and model size vary. It uses downstream task performance and training loss rather than held-out language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The scaling results are reported in figures, with qualitative trends described in the text; most figure values are not stated numerically in the text. Baseline comparisons and ablations unrelated to scaling are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps EEG pretraining data (1k–9k hours) and EEGSSM model size. It reports pretraining training loss and downstream kappa, F1 and balanced accuracy as these grow. That bears on scaling in a non-text modality (V5) and on downstream gains with scale (V6). It fits no power law, tests no extrapolation and finds no compute-optimal split. All values are figure-only.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that more EEG pretraining data and model capacity give consistent but diminishing downstream gains and lower training loss, with task-dependent plateaus (SEED-V). They suggest EEG models may keep benefiting from scaling, as in vision and language, and pick the 8-layer 15.17M model as the performance/efficiency balance.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales an EEG foundation model and reports downstream classification metrics and training loss; it does not use the original language-model held-out-loss measurement or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling response varies by downstream dataset: SEED-V plateaus after 5k hours of data and beyond 13.5M parameters, whereas FACED and ISRUC S3 are described as improving steadily over the tested ranges.
record.problems: Scaling sweep values are presented in figures without numerical values stated in the text. The scaling metrics are downstream performance and training loss, not held-out pretraining loss. The study does not fit power laws or test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocations. Model-size ranges are described differently in different sections.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling rows were omitted. The study's other downstream baseline comparisons, tokenizer/module ablations, and efficiency analyses do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute is not tested.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is derived.
Depth and width are varied together with parameter count, never at fixed parameter count.

No power-law form is fitted. Held-out loss is not reported. The data range is under one order of magnitude, and no compute axis is used. Image/video, repeated-data laws and transfer laws are not tested.
No quantitative prediction of downstream performance from scale or from pretraining loss is made, and no extrapolation. The downstream size sweep spans only about 2x in parameters.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices is made.

record.verdict_notes: Results are qualitative and figure-only, with no fitted exponents, which makes this weak evidence. The paper calls these 'scaling laws', but no functional form is fitted. Model-size descriptions conflict across Sec 3.4, N intro, N.2 and Table 23. Downstream size scaling covers only 3–8 layers, while the loss curves cover up to 24 layers. Pretraining runs only 10 epochs, and the loss is training loss, not held-out loss. Removed the V5 links from the downstream rows, moved the training-loss rows r7 and r8 from fits_no_version to V5, and emptied fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit laws on small runs and compare predictions with much larger runs.
It does not find a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute or test how that allocation changes with compute.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

The EEG scaling experiments vary data volume and model size, but do not fit or establish the same power-law form for held-out pretraining loss. Other modalities and regimes, including image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer-law fits, are not tested.
The study reports downstream performance trends with scale, but does not test quantitative prediction from pretraining loss or extrapolation from small runs.
It does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups or fitting choices. Downstream performance plateaus are not tests of curvature in held-out pretraining loss.

relationships.condition: EEGSSM pretraining training loss vs data volume, 1k–9k hours, TUEG
relationships.reason: Loss falls with data but with diminishing returns. The range is under one order of magnitude, uses training loss and has no power-law fit, so the power-law form is unverified (r7).
relationships.display_finding: Training loss decreased with diminishing returns over less than one order of magnitude in data, without a fitted power law.

relationships.condition: EEGSSM pretraining training loss vs model size, 3–24 layers (~4M–147M)
relationships.reason: Loss falls from 3 to 6 layers, then saturates beyond 7 layers; the >100M-parameter model gives no significant further reduction. This is a bend away from steady scaling (r8).
relationships.display_finding: Loss fell from 3 to 6 layers, saturated beyond 7 layers, and showed no significant further reduction above 100M parameters.

relationships.condition: FACED and ISRUC S3, data 1k–9k hours and model 3–8 layers
relationships.reason: The text reports steady downstream gains across the full tested range of data and model size (r1, r2, r4, r5). Figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Downstream performance improves steadily across the tested 1,000–9,000 training hours and 3–8 model layers on FACED and ISRUC S3.

relationships.reason: Gains are modest and plateau after 5k hours and beyond 13.5M parameters, so scaling benefit is task-dependent (r3, r6).
relationships.display_finding: Gains were modest and plateaued after 5k training hours and beyond 13.5M parameters.
